title: Virtual Prototyping and Experimental Assessment of Gating-System Optimization for Rapid Investment Casting of Miniaturized Cu–Al–Mn Shape Memory Alloy Helical Springs
abstract: Abstract This study investigates the optimization of a gating system for the rapid investment casting of miniaturized Cu-7.90Al-5.40Mn (wt.%) shape memory alloy helical springs by combining virtual prototyping through numerical simulation with representative casting trials. Sixteen simulation cases were examined as a function of primary runner-end geometry, injection direction, spring orientation, number of 0.70 mm vents, rotational speed (350–450 rpm), and pouring temperature (1039–1053 °C). The numerical analysis focused on recirculation, backflow-related mass loss, filling completeness, predicted void formation, misrun sensitivity, and shrinkage porosity. The results showed that the original spherical runner end promoted excessive recirculation and incomplete filling, whereas progressive redesign of the runner end substantially improved flow stabilization. Complete simulated filling without predicted void formation was obtained for the optimized runner-end design at 400 rpm/1043 °C and 450 rpm/1043 °C. Experimental castings using the optimized design showed markedly improved external integrity and filling quality relative to the baseline configuration, with the best overall experimental result obtained at 350 rpm/1053 °C. The cast-processed springs demonstrated successful thermomechanical actuation, where shape recovery is triggered by heating above 110 °C following initial deformation in the martensitic state at room temperature. Overall, the study demonstrates that modeling-based virtual prototyping is an effective tool for guiding gating-system redesign in the rapid investment casting of miniature Cu–Al–Mn SMA components, especially in geometries that are highly sensitive to backflow, gas evacuation, and local filling instability.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Shape memory alloys (SMAs) combine reversible strain recovery with a strongly nonlinear mechanical response, which makes them attractive for compact actuators, adaptive devices, damping systems, and other multifunctional components. Helical spring geometries are especially relevant because they can accommodate large displacements, operate in tension or compression, and transfer heat efficiently in thermally driven applications. 1 ,  2 – 3

In recent years, Cu–Al–Mn alloys have emerged as a cost-effective alternative to Ni–Ti for selected structural and functional applications. In parallel with this materials development, rapid investment casting has gained attention as a practical route for producing complex miniature SMA components that would be difficult or uneconomical to obtain by conventional machining. This route is particularly attractive for springs and lattice-like parts, but it also imposes demanding filling conditions because of thin sections, multiple curvature changes, and localized hook regions that are difficult to feed reliably. 4 ,  5 – 6

Within this context, the gating system becomes a central design variable. In miniature castings, modest changes in runner-end geometry, vent placement, rotational speed, or pouring temperature can strongly affect recirculation, air evacuation, mold filling, and defect formation. For this reason, virtual prototyping has become an increasingly valuable tool for the development of rapid investment casting routes, since it allows multiple design alternatives to be screened before physical trials are carried out. Commercial software-based modeling studies on Cu–Al–Mn castings have already shown that numerical simulation can identify flow-related weaknesses in miniature geometries and support the redesign of gating systems on a rational basis. 7 , 8

The present work builds on that perspective and focuses on a particularly demanding benchmark geometry: a miniaturized Cu–Al–Mn SMA helical tension spring. Rather than treating the spring primarily as a functional-material problem, the study is framed here as a metal-casting optimization problem in which the spring geometry provides a severe test of filling robustness. The central question is how the evolution of the runner-end design, combined with selected processing parameters, affects flow stabilization, filling completeness, defect-prone regions, and the practical castability of the component.

Accordingly, this study investigates how gating-system geometry and selected process parameters affect mold filling in the rapid investment casting of miniaturized Cu–Al–Mn shape memory alloy helical springs. Virtual prototyping using commercial modeling software was employed to compare 16 design and processing cases in terms of recirculation, backflow, filling completeness, predicted void formation, misrun sensitivity, and shrinkage porosity, and selected configurations were then examined experimentally by centrifugal casting. The objective was to identify a gating configuration capable of improving filling stability and reducing casting defects in this miniature geometry.

sections.heading: SMA, Part Geometry, and Rapid Investment Casting Concept
paragraphs: The component investigated in this study was a miniaturized helical tension spring designed according to the terminology adopted by Norton. 9  The detailed geometric characteristics of the spring used in the study are presented in Table  1 . Table  2  summarizes the nominal composition of the Cu-Al-Mn shape memory alloy used to manufacture the springs. No specific deoxidation treatment was applied prior to casting. However, prior to casting, all ingots underwent a cleaning procedure in an ultrasonic bath containing water and detergent for 5 minutes, followed by immersion in absolute alcohol for 10 minutes. Casting is carried out quickly (máx. 60 s) and under a protective argon flux. The rapid investment casting route employed centrifugal injection of molten metal into refractory plaster molds. These molds were shaped using 3D-printed resin patterns, clarifying that only the patterns, and not the molds, were 3D-printed. 7 , 8  The complete computational and experimental assembly comprised the crucible, a primary runner formed by a fixed standard base and an interchangeable runner-end region, flute-shaped secondary channels, cylindrical gates connecting the flutes to the spring, the spring cavities themselves, and the surrounding mold body. Figure  1  illustrates the main geometric elements used in the study. Figure 1 Geometry of the casting assembly used in the virtual prototyping study (a) primary runner base and runner-end region; (b) flutes, gates, and helical spring; (c) crucible, mold, and complete assembly .

sections.heading: Gating-system Variants and Simulation Matrix
paragraphs: Three main runner-end concepts were investigated. The baseline design consisted of a spherical end generated from a hemispherical revolution profile with a radius of 6.5 mm. Optimized design 1 used a more directional converging section with major radius 6.50 mm, minor radius 2.0 mm, length 9 mm, and a terminal hemisphere of radius 2.0 mm. Optimized design 2 retained the same concept but increased the converging length from 9 to 12 mm. Optimized design 3 employed a smoother transition from a 13 mm circular section to a 32 mm × 6 mm rectangular outlet positioned inside the flute region, with an axial transition length of 11 mm.

Sixteen simulation cases were defined in order to study the combined influence of runner-end geometry, injection direction, spring orientation, number of 0.70 mm vents, rotational speed, and pouring temperature, as detailed in Table  3 . The initial cases were used to diagnose the limitations of the original design, whereas the later cases progressively introduced design refinement and process-parameter changes. sections.heading: Process Modeling Setup and Analysis Criteria
paragraphs: The numerical study was carried out in ProCAST v16 10  within the Visual-Environment workflow. CAD geometries were generated in Autodesk Inventor and imported into the meshing module, where the computational domains were discretized using tetrahedral elements, Figure  2 . To improve numerical consistency across the simulation matrix, the meshing parameters adopted in this work were based on a grid-convergence workflow previously developed and applied by the research group for similar miniaturized casting geometries. The mesh quality was verified in two successive stages: first, by checking the surface discretization for geometric anomalies and poor-quality elements, and second, by evaluating the quality of the generated tetrahedral volumetric elements. Within this previously established framework, a refined element size of 0.30 mm was adopted for the helical spring segments. The same calibrated meshing strategy and dimensional criteria were then maintained for all simulated cases in order to preserve comparability among the results. Figure 2 Representative tetrahedral mesh of the computational domain showing the complete assembly (a) and the local refinement in the spring region (b).

The physical setup was defined in Visual-CAST. Thermophysical data for the Cu-based SMA were assigned through the software environment using the integrated CompuTherm thermodynamic database, which is based on the CALPHAD method. The alloy composition was Cu-7.90Al-5.40Mn (wt.%). The adopted liquidus and solidus temperatures were 1038 and 993 °C, respectively. To ensure simulation accuracy and reproducibility, the complete set of temperature-dependent thermophysical properties utilized for the alloy (thermal conductivity, density, enthalpy, solid fraction evolution, and dynamic viscosity) is explicitly detailed in the Supplementary Material (Figures  S6 - S11 ). The mold was assumed to be a refractory plaster mold initially at 420 °C. Its thermophysical properties were kept constant, as provided by the software database: a thermal conductivity of 0.58 W m −1  K −1 , a density of 1100 kg m −3 , and a specific heat capacity of 0.83836 kJ kg −1  K −1 . Room temperature was used for the external environment. The heat-transfer coefficients were 65.5 W m −2  K −1  between the mold and the environment and 535 W m −2  K −1  between the metal and the mold; the latter was kept constant based on estimated values validated in our previous work. 11  The total injected alloy mass was 19 g, and the rotation time was 11 s.

A centrifugal-casting preset was adopted in the simulation environment, with selected parameters adjusted to the specific problem. The realizable k–ε model was implemented because the present flow field involves strong rotation, severe recirculation, and localized flow separation. In comparison with the standard k–ε formulation, the realizable model provides a more suitable framework for such conditions by using a modified transport equation for the dissipation rate and a variable turbulent-viscosity formulation that satisfies realizability constraints. For this reason, it was considered more appropriate for describing the transient flow behavior associated with the present centrifugal-investment-casting configuration

Predicted voids were examined in three regions of the spring: central coils, support hooks oriented in the flow direction, and support hooks oriented opposite to the flow direction. This division was retained because the hooks opposite to the flow repeatedly emerged as the most difficult regions to fill and therefore served as a useful indicator of gating-system performance.

sections.heading: Experimental Casting of Selected Configurations
paragraphs: Representative experimental trials were carried out to compare the numerical trends with the macroscopic filling behavior observed in real castings. The Cu-7.90Al-5.40Mn alloy was first melted in an induction furnace to produce ingots. Spring patterns were fabricated in photopolymer castable resin using an AnyCubic Photon Mono SE printer and then invested in refractory plaster molds according to the rapid investment casting route adopted in this work. 7 , 8  The molds were fabricated using a commercial gypsum-bonded investment (Resincast) mixed at a water-to-powder ratio of 38 mL of distilled water per 100 g of powder. The slurry was manually homogenized and subsequently degassed under vacuum for 50 s using a KayaCast vacuum system to eliminate entrapped air. The mixture was then poured into the casting flasks containing the resin patterns while being mechanically vibrated on an orthopedic plaster vibrator to ensure complete cavity filling. The invested molds were allowed to bench-set and cure at room temperature for 90 min before the burnout process. The resin pattern removal and mold sintering were carried out in a resistance-heated muffle furnace following a multistage thermal cycle. The burnout process initiated with a heating ramp of 2.6 °C/min up to 240 °C, where it was held for 300 min for gradual resin degradation. The temperature was then increased at a rate of 4.0 °C/min to a peak sintering temperature of 750 °C, maintained for 240 min to ensure complete ash elimination and mold conditioning. Finally, the furnace was cooled down to 450 °C, which is the temperature at which the mold is transferred to the casting machine, and held for at least 60 min prior to the centrifugal injection.

The centrifugal-casting experiments were performed on a PowerCAST 1700 induction casting unit equipped with an integrated induction coil. For each experimental run, a solid charge of 19 g of the alloy (well within the equipment’s maximum capacity of 50 g) was placed directly inside the crucible, where it was melted in situ under the induction field, avoiding external pouring operations. The selected trials corresponded to the baseline spherical runner-end configuration under the nominal conditions of Case 1, and to two Optimized design 3 configurations corresponding to Cases 10 and 15. The pouring/injection temperatures followed the exact values established in the simulation matrix (Table  2 ): 1043 °C for Cases 1 and 10, and 1053 °C for Case 15. At the time of centrifugal injection, the refractory plaster molds remained preheated at the target casting temperature. The experimental comparison was based on visual examination of filling completeness, preservation of the hook geometry, apparent surface condition, and the presence or absence of visible casting discontinuities.

Representative experimental trials were carried out in replicate form for the selected casting conditions. At this stage, the experimental comparison should be understood as an exploratory assessment of practical repeatability in terms of macroscopic filling completeness, hook preservation, and visible external integrity, rather than as a statistically designed validation campaign. For this reason, the agreement between simulation and experiment is interpreted qualitatively, although the main macroscopic trends were reproducible across the replicate trials. At this stage, the experimental assessment was based on replicate casting trials intended to verify the reproducibility of the main macroscopic trends rather than to establish a statistically powered comparison of defect metrics. In addition, the optimized casting tree has continued to be employed in subsequent laboratory casting studies, including less dense Ni–Ti alloys, with satisfactory mold filling and helical spring production without visible external defects. These observations reinforce the practical repeatability of the optimized gating concept, although a full statistical analysis remains a subject for future work.

sections.heading: Results and Discussion
paragraphs: The results of the sixteen simulation cases, examining the influence of runner-end geometry, injection direction, and process parameters, are presented hereafter. As previously detailed in the simulation matrix (Table  3 ), these cases encompass the main controlled geometric and operational variables. Detailed visualizations of the gating-system iterations and additional filling patterns for all simulation cases are provided in the Supplementary Material.

sections.heading: Gating-System Evolution and Flow Stabilization
paragraphs: The early simulation cases made it clear that the baseline spherical runner end was not robust for the present miniature geometry. Cases 1–4 all showed excessive recirculation, backflow-related mass loss, and incomplete filling, as shown in Figure  3 . Figure 3 Representative baseline-flow behavior showing excessive recirculation and backflow-related mass loss for the spherical runner-end design.

Changing the injection direction from orthogonal to parallel relative to the spring axis did not remove this behavior, which indicates that the main limitation lay in the runner-end design rather than in spring orientation alone.

The first redesign step, represented by Optimized design 1, improved the flow path by introducing a more directional converging section (see Figures  S3  and  S4  in the Supplementary Material for geometry details). Under the 350 rpm/1043 °C conditions, this modification suppressed external mass loss in Cases 5–7, which is a clear improvement over the baseline. Even so, incomplete filling remained in critical spring regions, especially in the hooks opposite to the filling direction. Increasing the rotational speed to 400 rpm with the same design (Case 8) reintroduced excessive backflow, indicating that the stabilization length of this geometry was still insufficient for the more severe flow condition.

Optimized design 2 extended the converging length but did not fully resolve the problem at 400 rpm (Case 9). The most important improvement was obtained with Optimized design 3, which replaced the compact converging tip with a smoother transition from a circular to a rectangular outlet aligned with the flute region. For Cases 10–14, this design substantially reduced the severity of recirculation and, in most conditions, prevented mass loss to the external environment, as can be seen in Figure  4 . Cases 10 and 12 are particularly relevant because they combined stable flow behavior with complete simulated filling and no predicted void formation. Figure 4 Representative flow behavior for Optimized design 3, showing moderated recirculation without external mass loss: (a) Case 10 at t = 0.40 s; (b) Case 12 at t = 0.37 s.

The high-temperature cases further clarified the process window. Cases 15 and 16 showed favorable filling metrics, and the misrun-sensitivity index also improved under these conditions. However, the simulations still indicated undesirable flow events associated with abrupt gas release and/or renewed mass loss. This means that higher pouring temperature can improve castability, but it should not be interpreted in isolation from flow stability. A consolidated interpretation of the simulated flow and filling outcomes for all cases is provided in Table  4 . Table 4 Consolidated Interpretation of the Simulated Flow and Filling Outcomes Case or case group Flow stability Mass loss Filling outcome Critical region(s) Interpretation 1–4 Excessive recirculation Yes Incomplete Hooks opposite to flow; additional defects in some orientations Baseline spherical runner end is unsuitable for the spring geometry. 5–7 Recirculation reduced relative to baseline No Still incomplete Hooks opposite to flow; occasional coil defect Optimized design 1 improved flow stabilization, but gas evacuation remained insufficient. 8 Excessive recirculation Yes Incomplete One central coil Higher speed exceeded the stabilization capability of Optimized design 1. 9 Intense recirculation Yes Incomplete One central coil Longer converging length helped, but did not eliminate instability at 400 rpm. 10 Moderate recirculation No Complete No predicted voids Optimized design 3 provided the most balanced simulated condition. 11 Low recirculation No Incomplete Upper coil and lower hook Lower speed with optimized design 3 was less favorable than Case 10. 12 Moderate recirculation No Complete No predicted voids A second fully filled simulated condition obtained with Optimized design 3. 13–14 Moderate recirculation No Incomplete Hooks opposite to flow; one adjacent hook Reducing pouring temperature narrowed the process window. 15 Excessive flow event Yes Complete No predicted voids in filling map Higher temperature improved filling, but with renewed backflow-related mass loss. 16 Flow instability associated with gas release Yes Complete No predicted voids in filling map High temperature improved sensitivity metrics, but practical robustness still requires caution.

sections.heading: Filling Completeness and Location of Critical Regions
paragraphs: Once the strongest recirculation problems were reduced, the simulations consistently pointed to the same critical geometry features: The support hooks oriented against the filling direction and, under some conditions, isolated spring coils, as exemplified by the results in Figures  5  and  6 . This trend is important from a metal-casting perspective because it shows that local flow exhaustion and gas evacuation at the extremities of the cavity are more difficult to control than filling of the central body of the spring. Comprehensive void distribution maps for the intermediate design cases are available in the Supplementary Material (Figures  S13 – S19 ). Figure 5 Simulated filling result for Case 1, showing incomplete cavity filling and predicted void formation. (a) Front view; (b) rear isometric view. Figure 6 Simulated filling result for Case 5, also showing incomplete cavity filling and predicted void formation. (a) Front view; (b) rear isometric view.

The filling maps associated with Cases 10 and 12 are particularly significant because they show that complete simulated filling without predicted void formation can be achieved when the runner-end geometry promotes smoother flow transfer into the secondary channels, as illustrated in Figures  7  and  8 , respectively. By contrast, Cases 11, 13, and 14 indicate that the same general gating concept becomes less effective when the balance among rotational speed, pouring temperature, and flow stability is altered. Figure 7 Simulated filling result for Case 10, showing complete cavity filling without predicted void formation. (a) Front view; (b) rear isometric view. Figure 8 Simulated filling result for Case 12, also showing complete cavity filling without predicted void formation. (a) Front view; (b) rear isometric view.

The high-temperature cases should be interpreted with some care. Cases 15 and 16 exhibited complete simulated filling and favorable misrun indicators, but the same simulations also suggested that the process may become more sensitive to abrupt gas release or excessive flow return under these conditions (further detailed in Figures  S11  and  S12  of the Supplementary Material). From an engineering standpoint, this means that the best practical solution is not necessarily the case with the lowest numerical sensitivity alone; rather, it is the configuration that best balances filling completeness and flow robustness.

sections.heading: Misrun Sensitivity and Shrinkage Porosity
paragraphs: In addition to the direct filling outputs, the study considered misrun sensitivity and shrinkage porosity. These indicators do not describe exactly the same aspect of process performance as filling completeness or backflow-related mass loss. The sensitivity map identifies regions that remain difficult to fill under the imposed conditions, whereas backflow and abrupt gas release represent additional flow phenomena that can influence the practical outcome. For this reason, the different indicators should be interpreted together rather than independently, as summarized in the consolidated results of Table  5 . Table 5 Misrun-Sensitivity Classification and Predicted Shrinkage Porosity Volumes from the ProCAST Analysis Case Misrun sensitivity 15% cutoff porosity (cm 3 ) 20% cutoff porosity (cm 3 ) 25% cutoff porosity (cm 3 ) 30% cutoff porosity (cm 3 ) 1–7 Poor/Very poor Not evaluated Not evaluated Not evaluated Not evaluated 8 Poor 8.79 × 10 −5 7.73 × 10 −5 0 8.79 × 10 −5 9 Poor Not evaluated Not evaluated Not evaluated Not evaluated 10 Poor 6.36 × 10 −5 6.36 × 10 −5 3.707 × 10 −5 6.36 × 10 −5 11 Poor 5.28 × 10 −5 5.28 × 10 −5 4.11 × 10 −5 5.28 × 10 −5 12 Poor 6.36 × 10 −5 6.36 × 10 −5 6.36 × 10 −5 6.36 × 10 −5 13 Very poor 6.56 × 10 −5 5.95 × 10 −5 5.95 × 10 −5 6.56 × 10 −5 14 Very poor 12.7 × 10 −5 12.1 × 10 −5 10.7 × 10 −5 12.7 × 10 −5 15 Good 5.27 × 10 −5 5.06 × 10 −5 5.06 × 10 −5 5.27 × 10 −5 16 Good 8.10 × 10 −6 8.10 × 10 −6 0 8.10 × 10 −6

The predicted shrinkage porosity volumes in Cases 8–14 were generally on the order of 10 −5  cm 3  in the spring coils and hooks, while Case 16 reached 8.10 × 10 −6  cm 3  at the 15% cutoff. The simulations repeatedly placed these porosity concentrations near the hook and link regions (Figure  9 ), which is consistent with the fact that these are the geometrically most constrained regions of the spring cavity. In relative terms, Case 14 exhibited the highest predicted porosity level, whereas Cases 15 and 16 showed the most favorable sensitivity classification. Figure 9 Representative spatial distribution of predicted shrinkage porosity in the spring links and hooks. (a) Case 14; (b) Case 16.

Even so, the cases with the best misrun-sensitivity classification were not free from other flow issues. When comparing the sensitivity map of the baseline configuration (Figure  10 ), which shows a high risk of failure, with the optimized design (Figure  11 ), a significant improvement is noted, although some points with limited filling risk remain. The peak evolution is observed under high-temperature conditions (Figure  12 ), where the part exhibits vast regions of zero risk and very few links with limited risk. Figure 10 Representative misrun-sensitivity map for the baseline spherical runner-end configuration (Case 1). (a) Top isometric view; (b) bottom isometric view. Figure 11 Representative misrun-sensitivity map for Optimized design 3 under the conditions corresponding to Case 10. (a) Top isometric view; (b) bottom isometric view. Figure 12 Representative misrun-sensitivity maps for the high-temperature conditions: (a) Case 15; (b) Case 16.

This reinforces a practical design lesson: A satisfactory gating system for miniature castings should combine low defect sensitivity with stable filling and limited backflow, rather than maximizing any one numerical metric in isolation.

sections.heading: Experimental Comparison with Representative Simulated Cases
paragraphs: The experimental castings were consistent with the main tendencies predicted by the numerical study as summarized in Table  6 . Table 6 Qualitative Comparison between Representative Numerical Predictions and Experimental Observations Representative condition Main numerical indication Main experimental observation Engineering interpretation Baseline spherical runner end (nominally matching Case 1) Excessive recirculation, mass loss, incomplete filling, critical hook regions Visible underfill in hooks opposite to the flow direction; wrinkled external appearance The baseline runner-end design is not robust for the miniature spring. Optimized design 3, 400 rpm, 1043 °C (Case 10) Moderate recirculation, no mass loss, complete simulated filling, no predicted voids No visible filling interruption; improved macroscopic integrity and shape retention This condition represents the most balanced simulated operating window. Optimized design 3, 350 rpm, 1053 °C (Case 15) Good misrun sensitivity and complete simulated filling, but with flow events associated with mass loss Best overall surface and dimensional quality among the tested castings Higher pouring temperature can be beneficial, provided that flow stability is monitored.

The baseline configuration manufactured with the original spherical runner end under the nominal Case 1 conditions showed visible filling defects in the hooks oriented opposite to the flow direction, as can be seen in Figure  13 . These defects coincide with the regions that the simulation had already identified as the most critical. Figure 13 Representative casting obtained with the baseline spherical runner-end design, showing visible filling defects in hooks opposite to the flow direction.

By contrast, the component cast with Optimized design 3 under the nominal Case 10 conditions showed no visible macroscopic voids or filling interruptions and exhibited a noticeably better external geometry than the baseline casting, as shown in Figure  14 . This observation is consistent with the complete simulated filling obtained for Case 10 and with the more favorable flow behavior associated with the redesigned runner end. Figure 14 Representative casting obtained with Optimized design 3 at 1043 °C and 400 rpm, showing improved filling quality and geometric integrity.

The casting produced under the nominal Case 15 conditions, presented in Figure  15 , exhibited the best overall surface and dimensional quality among the experimentally examined parts. This experimental result is compatible with the improved filling sensitivity predicted at higher pouring temperature. At the same time, the simulation suggests that high-temperature conditions should still be considered together with flow-stability indicators, since the numerical results also pointed to backflow-related events in this regime. Figure 15 Representative casting obtained with Optimized design 3 at 1053 °C and 350 rpm, showing the best overall macroscopic quality among the experimentally examined parts.

Taken together, the experimental results support the use of the virtual-prototyping workflow as a design-guidance tool. The agreement should be interpreted as qualitative, but it is sufficiently consistent to show that the model captured the main differences between the baseline and optimized gating concepts.

To demonstrate that the Cu-Al-Mn alloy springs in this study exhibit functional shape memory effect properties, the casting tree shown in Figure  15  was subjected to heat treatment at 850 °C for 1 hour and quenched in water at room temperature. A small specimen was then removed from one of the hook vent rods and characterized via differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), revealing phase transformation peaks during cooling (M s  to M f  temperatures) and heating (A s  to A f  temperatures), as shown in Figure  16 . Figure 16 DSC thermogram of the spring obtained with Optimized design 3 at 1053 °C and 350 rpm.

Therefore, Figure  16  reveals a reversible martensitic transformation occurring between 34.1 °C (M f ) and 107.2 °C (A f ), with transformation enthalpy (ΔH) values consistent with those observed in Cu-based shape memory alloys. 5 , 12  In practice, this result implies that if the spring from Fig.  15  is plastically deformed in tension at room temperature (T < M f , martensite) and subsequently heated to approximately 110 °C (T > A f , austenite), it will recover its original length through spontaneous contraction. This characterizes the cast-processed component as a natural thermomechanical actuator.

sections.heading: Practical Implications for the Casting of Miniature SMA Springs
paragraphs: The study indicates that runner-end geometry exerted a stronger first-order effect on casting performance than changes in spring orientation. Venting improved local filling in some cases, but it did not compensate for an intrinsically unstable runner-end design. Once the runner-end concept was corrected, the process became much less sensitive to global flow breakdown and the analysis could focus on local defect-prone regions.

For the present geometry, the most persistent critical regions were the hook extremities opposite to the filling direction and selected spring coils. These locations should therefore be treated as priority regions in future gating studies on similar miniature parts. More broadly, the results show that successful casting of small Cu–Al–Mn SMA springs depends on coordinated control of flow stability, gas evacuation, and local feeding rather than on increasing temperature or speed alone.

From the standpoint of process development, the main contribution of the work is methodological. The numerical simulation workflow enabled the original gating concept to be screened, redesigned, and narrowed to a smaller set of physically meaningful casting trials. Even when the final experimental assessment is based on macroscopic part quality, this strategy remains valuable because it reduces trial-and-error development and concentrates physical experimentation on the most promising design space. Although this experimental validation relies primarily on a qualitative macroscopic assessment of filling completeness and surface integrity, this approach provides immediate and unambiguous evidence of the gating system’s effectiveness. The transition from severe misruns and incomplete profiles to geometrically sound helical springs demonstrates the practical success of the proposed redesign. Nevertheless, quantitative characterizations such as micro-computed tomography for internal porosity distribution and high-resolution dimensional metrology constitute essential steps for full process industrialization and are planned for future stages of this research.

Although Optimized design 3 provided the most balanced response within the present study, this gating concept should not be interpreted as universally optimal. Its performance was established only for the specific combination of Cu–7.90Al–5.40Mn alloy, spring geometry, refractory plaster mold, mold preheating condition, injected mass, and centrifugal-casting window investigated here. Even under the optimized concept, the hook extremities opposite to the filling direction remained the most sensitive local regions, and higher pouring temperature, while beneficial for filling, could still reintroduce flow-instability events such as backflow or abrupt gas release. In addition, the present experimental assessment is limited to macroscopic filling quality and visible external integrity; internal porosity and fine dimensional deviations were not quantified. Therefore, application of the proposed gating configuration to other alloys, dimensions, or mold systems should be regarded as a starting design concept requiring case-specific numerical and experimental re-optimization.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: This study used virtual prototyping and representative casting trials to optimize the gating system for rapid investment casting of miniaturized Cu–Al–Mn shape memory alloy helical springs across a matrix of 16 distinct numerical simulation cases.

The baseline spherical runner-end design promoted excessive recirculation, backflow-related mass loss, and incomplete filling, demonstrating that it was not adequate for the present miniature spring geometry.

Progressive redesign of the runner end substantially improved flow behavior. Optimized design 3 provided the most balanced simulated response, and Cases 10 and 12 achieved complete simulated filling (100%) without predicted void formation.

The combined interpretation of filling maps, misrun sensitivity, and shrinkage porosity showed that the hook regions opposite to the flow direction were the most persistent critical zones of the casting. Quantifying these defects revealed that the optimized runner design under high-temperature parameters (Case 16) successfully suppressed local shrinkage porosity to a minimum volume of 8.10 × 10 −6  cm 3  at a 15% cutoff threshold, shifting the misrun-sensitivity metric from “very poor” to “good.”

Experimental castings were qualitatively consistent with the simulated trends: The baseline design produced visible hook defects, whereas the optimized design yielded markedly better macroscopic integrity and filling quality. The best experimental result was obtained at 350 rpm and 1053 °C.

Functional testing of the spring from the optimized casting tree, validated by DSC analysis, demonstrated the successful development of a thermomechanical actuator triggered by room-temperature deformation and subsequent heating above 110 °C.

Overall, the results demonstrate that numerical simulation-based virtual prototyping is an effective design-support tool for the rapid investment casting of miniature Cu–Al–Mn SMA components and can significantly improve gating-system development for geometries that are highly sensitive to local filling instability.
